See what is written in Job: "no one is clean from filth, not even if his life should be of a single day". He did not say: "no one is clean from sin," but: "no one is clean from filth". For filth and sins do not signify the same thing; and that you may know that filth means one thing and sin another, Isaiah teaches most plainly, saying: "the Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and will cleanse the blood from their midst, by the spirit of judgment the filth and by the spirit of burning the blood". Every soul that has been clothed with a human body has its own "filth". And that you may know that Jesus too was made filthy by his own will, because for our salvation he had assumed a human body, listen to the prophet Zechariah saying: "Jesus was clothed with filthy garments".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 14

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: When one has recognized the differences in sins, one can see how the Lord says in Isaiah, "The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion and will cleanse the blood from their midst by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning." Filth is washed away by a spirit of judgment. Blood is washed away by a spirit of burning. Even if you have not committed a sin that leads to death, you have still sinned and have thereby become filthy. The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and he will cleanse the blood from among them. A spirit of judgment will be the recompense for filth, and a spirit of burning will be a recompense for the blood. Whenever we commit heinous sins, we do not need lye or washing with soap; rather we need the spirit of burning.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And truly he was "a horn of salvation in the house of David", because this prophecy is sung in harmony: "For a vineyard was made on a horn". On what horn? On Christ Jesus, on him of whom it is now written: "he raised up a horn of salvation for us, in the house of David his servant, as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 10

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: See then how very bad sinning is, that they may be delivered to Satan, who holds captive the souls of those forsaken by God—though God does not forsake without cause or judgment those whom he has abandoned. For when he sends the rain for the vineyard and the vineyard bears thorns instead of grapes, what else will God do except order the clouds not to sprinkle rain on the vineyard?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: See then how very bad sinning is, that they may be delivered to Satan, who holds captive the souls of those forsaken by God—though God does not forsake without cause or judgment those whom he has abandoned. For when he sends the rain for the vineyard and the vineyard bears thorns instead of grapes, what else will God do except order the clouds not to sprinkle rain on the vineyard?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: So long as "King Uzziah" lived, the prophet Isaiah could not "see the vision". For "Uzziah" was a sinner, "doing what was wicked before the sight of the Lord", and acting against the will of the divine law. "He entered the temple" and the holy of holies, and for this reason he was covered with "leprosy on his forehead", so that, going outside the city, he was reckoned among the unclean. Such a ruler of the soul, therefore, must die, that we may be able "to see the vision" of God; for not in vain is it written: "and it came to pass in the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord". For each one of us "Uzziah" is alive, or Pharaoh, and we do not "groan" while doing the "works" of Egypt. But if he "dies", then we "groan", as it is written in Exodus. If "Uzziah" lives, we do not "see the glory of God"; but if he "dies", then we "see"—as soon as "Uzziah dies"—"the glory of God", provided only that the Word "reign" in us, the Word who said: "but I have been appointed king by him", and that wrath does not "reign". Indeed there is also a "king" of "sin"; the Apostle, knowing this, says: "let sin therefore not reign in your mortal body". Wretched is that man in whom "sin reigns", who hands himself over to such a "king", despising the kingdom of God and subjecting himself to pleasure. Therefore the lover of pleasure is not a lover of God, and according to the Apostle it is said of certain persons: "loving pleasure more than God". And indeed this very thing was said not of those who are entirely unbelievers, but of those who dwell within, "loving pleasure more than God, having a semblance of piety but denying its power". These things are said on account of the death of "King Uzziah", after whose demise the prophet says he "saw the vision". But what is the "vision"? "I saw the Lord seated upon a throne lofty and exalted". Not everyone who "sees the Lord" "sees" him "seated upon a throne lofty and exalted". I know that another prophet "saw the Lord" and "saw" him "seated upon a throne", but not "lofty" nor "exalted". Expounding the Scripture, Daniel says: "thrones were placed", and that "throne" was not "lofty". And: "I will come to sit in judgment over the people in the valley of Jehoshaphat". Therefore here he "sat in the valley", and "in the valley" when he is about "to judge", when he is about to condemn. But it is another thing "to see him seated upon a throne lofty and exalted". And in Micah "God goes forth and descends". And in order to see Sodom, "he descends": "Descending", he says, "I will see whether they have carried out to the full according to the cry of them that comes to me". God, therefore, is sometimes seen above, sometimes below, according to the dignity of the matters at hand. "I saw the Lord", then, Isaiah says, "seated upon a throne lofty and exalted". If I "see God" reigning over those who are here, I do not "see" him "upon a throne lofty and exalted"; if I "see" him "reigning" over the heavenly powers, I "see" him "upon a throne lofty and exalted". What do I mean by the heavenly powers? "Thrones, dominions, principalities, powers" are the heavenly powers. And if I "see" him, how he "reigns" over these in the Word, "I saw the Lord seated upon a throne lofty and exalted". "And the house was full of his glory". On high, where his "throne" is "exalted", "the house is also full of his glory". I do not think that this house which is on earth "is full of glory". "The Lord's is the earth and the fullness thereof". But the "fullness of the glory of God" you will not find in the present; yet if anyone builds a temple to God, the "glory of God" will be seen, and if he keeps what has been said, "the house" will be seen to be "full of the glory of God". But I do not know whether the "house" is filled with "glory" in this way. And in Leviticus, insofar as concerns the present, not yet—but, God granting, it will be read in the assembly that follows—it is said that the Lord commanded certain things to be done, that the "glory of the Lord" might be seen. Nor will the "glory of God" ever appear if these things are not done. And we shall come to know those things when they have been read.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "It came to pass", he says, "in the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord of Sabaoth sitting upon a throne high and lifted up". The "vision" is recorded; why is the time of the king signified? Give heed to when the "vision" arose: when "King Uzziah died", Isaiah "saw the Lord of Sabaoth sitting upon a throne high and lifted up". If any of us knows who "Uzziah" was and what he did, he can know what the prophet taught through the Spirit, what the divine word sets forth for us. I will go to the life of "King Uzziah" and inquire from the books of Kingdoms and from the history of Chronicles concerning "Uzziah", and there I see that it is necessary, if it is to come to pass that "I should see the Lord of Sabaoth sitting upon a throne high and lifted up", that "King Uzziah" must "die" for me. This "Uzziah", descending from the seed of David and "reigning" over the people of Judah, as long indeed as "Zechariah, who had understanding" lived — for so it is written in the second book of Chronicles — "did what was right in the sight of the Lord". And not content with this, he made great lights for the Lord and set the temple of God in order, and many were his virtues in religion. But when "Zechariah who had understanding" died, then he did evil. Do you wish to know this evil that he did? He was a king, not a priest (one is the royal order, another the priestly order); he wished to "enter into the temple" and to perform the place of a priest and to do a work which had not been granted to him; he "entered in", forestalling the priests, and took the "vessel of libation". But there entered also the "chief of the priests" who was at that time, "and eighty priests with him"; "the chief of the priests said to him": are you not Uzziah, and not a priest? He violently persisted, "and leprosy went up upon his forehead"; he was cast out as dead, he "went out" of the temple, the Lord led him out. Therefore he became a "leper" because of his transgression of the law. Each one is under a kingdom, whether of "sin" or of righteousness. If "sin reigns" in me, I am one of the kings of Israel who "entered the temple" violently; if I am righteous according to the measure of my progress and do what is right and persevere before the sight of God, righteousness "reigns" in me. But as long as the "leper" lived, Isaiah had "unclean lips"; as long as the wicked man lived, Isaiah could not "see the Lord of Sabaoth" and had "unclean lips"; for he was under a wicked king. But when does he begin to "see the vision" of God? "In the year in which Uzziah died". Things similar to these you will be able to learn also from many scriptures, God granting it. In Exodus something of this kind is written: "and it came to pass after many days, the king of Egypt died, and the children of Israel groaned, and their cry went up to God". As long as Pharaoh lived, the "children of Israel" did "not groan", and, placed under punishments, they did not even have the free faculty of "groaning"; for the king was alive, who commanded them to make "bricks and straw". As long as Pharaoh lived, they did "not groan to God"; when Pharaoh died, then they had the strength to lift up their faces wet with weeping. The wicked king lives in our breast as long as Pharaoh the devil lives. Then we labor at "bricks" and "straw", then we swallow our tears in silence and do the first works of iniquity; but when he has died, at the visitation of the Lord our God, then we "groan to the Lord". Therefore let us pray that the kingdom of "sin, which is in our mortal body", may die. For it says: "sin was dead, but I lived"; and again: "sin revived, but I died". When "Uzziah", who holds the kingdom of "sin", "dies", Pharaoh too "dies". When the most wicked "king dies", I lift my eyes to heaven and God hears my voice, as he did for Abraham and Isaac and Jacob; and "I see the Lord of Sabaoth sitting" and reigning "upon a high throne", whom the people did not see; for "Uzziah had not yet died". I wish to insert something similar concerning the good thing, which is contrary to this. This very "Uzziah", as long as "Zechariah who had understanding" lived, "did not sin in the sight of God"; when Zechariah died he turned aside from the Lord, at the time when he was ruling over the people and governing the city. And, reading these things by day and by night and hearing the Lord say: "you ought to have put the money on the table, and I at my coming would have exacted it with interest", let us not gather up "in a napkin the mina" entrusted to us, nor let us "put the money on the table", but let us lend it out to the peoples. And when we have entrusted the Lord's account to you, it will have to be seen how you will pay back what was entrusted "with interest". Amen!

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: It is impossible to find the beginning of God. The beginning of God's movement you can nowhere grasp—not you, I say, and not anyone else, nor any other of the things that have subsistence. The Savior alone and the Holy Spirit, who have always been with God, see His "face"; and perhaps also the "angels", who "continually see the face of the Father who is in heaven", see also the beginnings of His works. And so too before men "the Seraphim hide their feet"; for the "last things", such as they are, cannot be recounted. "Who has announced concerning the last things?" says the Scripture. The things that we see—granting even that we do see something—are the middle things. What existed before the world we do not know; yet certain things did exist before the world. What is to follow after the world we do not apprehend for certain; yet other things will be after the world. Those things, therefore, that are written—"in the beginning God made heaven and earth. But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss; and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters"—these are apprehended; those "waters", over which the "Spirit of God" brooded, belonged to the world. But also the "darkness", which "was over the abyss", is not unbegotten; for both were created out of nothing. Hear God saying in Isaiah: "I am God, who framed light and made darkness". Hear wisdom proclaiming in Proverbs: "before all the abysses I was born". These were not unbegotten; but when or how they were born, I do not know. For by the "Seraphim" are "veiled" the first of God's works, that is, the "face of God"; and likewise also the "feet". The things that after the last age are to be for ages of ages, who can expound? It belongs to garrulous men to promise knowledge of these things—men who do not know that a human being can grasp only those things that are the middle things. And the things that after the world, up to the consummation, are to be in the judgment—concerning the punishments, concerning the recompense—of these too many things are hidden from us. This is because of what is written: "with two they veiled the face". But not only did they "veil", they also "covered over", that is, "veiled", so that neither might even a little of the first things be seen—I mean of the "face"—nor might even a little of the "last things" be recognized, that is, of His "feet". "And with two they were flying". The middle things are laid open for contemplation.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And the Seraphim stood round about him, six wings to the one, and six wings to the other". I see two "Seraphim", each of them having in itself "six wings". Then the arrangement of the "wings". "And with two wings indeed they covered the face"—not their own, but God's—"and with two wings they covered the feet"—not their own, but God's—"and with two wings they were flying". According to what is written, it seems contradictory: if they "stood", they could not "fly". But it is written: "they stood round about him, six wings to the one and six wings to the other; and with two they covered the face and with two they covered the feet, and with two they were flying; and they cried one to another". Truly these "Seraphim", who are around God, who by knowledge alone say: "Holy, Holy, Holy!", on this account keep the mystery of the Trinity, because they too are holy; for among all the things that are, nothing is holier than these. And not lightly do they say "one to another": "Holy, Holy, Holy!", but they proclaim with a cry the confession that is salutary for all. What are these two "Seraphim"? My Lord Jesus and the Holy Spirit. And do not think that the nature of the Trinity is divided, if the functions of the names are preserved. "They covered the face" of God; for the beginning of God is unknown. But also the "feet"; for what last thing is comprehended in our God? Only the middle things are seen; what was before these, I do not know. From the things that are, I understand God; what will come after these, insofar as they are to come, I do not know. "Who has declared it to him?" said Ecclesiastes. "Announce to me the first things and the last things that shall be, and I will say that you are gods", said Isaiah. From which, if anyone should tell the "past things" and be able to tell the "last things", he is "God"; who, then, can tell them except the "Seraphim"? Who can say: "Holy, Holy, Holy!" except the "Seraphim"? But they laid bare which part of God, so to speak—his middle—and "they cried one to the other", standing beside God "and saying": "Holy, Holy, Holy!". They "stand", therefore, and are moved; they "stand" with God, they are moved in making God known; for understand that "they cover the face, they cover the feet"—they do not move the things that are covered, they do not "cover" the things with which "they fly". And they say: "Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord of Sabaoth, the whole earth is full of his glory". The coming of my Lord Jesus Christ is announced; and so now "the whole earth is full of his glory". Or else it is not yet "full", but it is to come to pass that it be filled, when that prayer shall have been fulfilled by which the Lord himself commanded us to "pray" to the "Father", saying: "when you pray, say: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name! Thy kingdom come! Thy will be done, as in heaven so on earth!". As yet the "will" of the "Father" is "in heaven"; "on earth" his "will" is not yet fulfilled; and Jesus himself, according to the dispensation of the flesh which he had put on, says: "he gave me all power, as in heaven so on earth"—not that he did not have "power on earth", he who had it "in heaven", and that he received something of the world, he who "had come into his own", but that God might so be believed "on earth" as he was believed "in heaven"; therefore the man Christ received "power" which before he did not have, and up to the present he does not yet have "power" over all "on earth". For over those who sin he does not yet reign; but when the "power" over these too has been given to him, when "all things have been made subject" to him, then the "power" will be complete and he will go about "subjecting all things to himself". But some do not yet wish to be "made subject" to him, but as yet are "subjected" to his enemies. Let us, moreover, say: "shall not my soul be made subject to God? for from him is my salvation".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: My Hebrew master used to say that the two seraphim, which are described in Isaiah as having six wings each and as crying one to another and saying, "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts," were to be understood to mean the only-begotten Son of God and the Holy Spirit.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: My Hebrew teacher also used to teach as follows, that since the beginning or the end of all things could not be comprehended by any except our Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit, this was the reason why Isaiah spoke of there being in the vision that appeared to him two seraphim only, who with two wings cover the face of God, with two cover his feet and with two fly, crying one to another and saying, "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of your glory." For because the two seraphim alone have their wings over the face of God and over his feet, we may venture to declare that neither the armies of the holy angels, nor the holy thrones, nor the dominions, nor principalities nor powers can wholly know the beginnings of all things and the ends of the universe.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
"And they cried out one to another", not "one" to many, but "one to another". For to hear the holiness of God, which is announced by the Savior, according to the dignity of the matter no one can except the Holy Spirit; just as, in turn, to indwell the sanctity of God, which is announced by the Holy Spirit, no one can except the Savior alone. On this account "they cried out one to another and said: Holy, Holy, Holy!" It does not suffice for them to cry 'Holy!' once, nor twice, but they take up the perfect number of the Trinity, that they may manifest the multitude of the holiness of God, which is the repeated commonalty of a threefold holiness; to the holiness of the Father is joined the holiness of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. "For both He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all of one". He who "sanctifies" is the Savior, according to this—that as a man He receives holiness from God the Father. And so they say: "Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord of Sabaoth!". And "Sabaoth" is interpreted, as Aquila has handed down, the Lord of armies.

"The whole earth is full of His glory". Once the "house" was full of "glory", but now to those who are upon the "earth" it is prophesied by the Seraphim that it shall come to pass that Christ will fill "the whole earth" with the "glory" of God. For in all who by their manner of life glorify God, there is "His glory", and thus "the whole earth is full of the glory" of God. Once "the whole earth was" not "full of the glory" of God, but one corner of the earth, when it was said: "God is known in Judea, in Israel His name is great". Glory be to God, "who sent His Son", that "the whole earth might become full of His glory". But what does it profit you if the "earth" is "full" of the "glory" of God because of the churches of the blessed who are everywhere, but you yourself are not a partaker of the "glory" of the "fullness of God"? You too, therefore, labor and strive in all things, seeking the "glory" of God, that it may dwell and find a place also in you, and that you too may become, together with "the whole earth" in which is the "glory" of God, "full of His glory". How does the fullness of the "glory" of God come about through each one of us? If the things I do, the things I speak, are done unto the "glory" of God, then my word and my act become "full" of the "glory" of God. If both my going out and my coming in are unto the "glory" of God, if my food, if my drink, if "all" that I do "is done unto the glory of God", then I too am a partaker of this saying: "the earth is full of His glory".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And with two they were flying, and they said one to another: Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord of Sabaoth, the whole earth is full of his glory. And the lintel was lifted up by the voice with which they cried", by the "voice" of Jesus Christ and the "voice" of the Holy Spirit. If any one of us hears the "voice" of Jesus Christ and of the Holy Spirit "crying out", the "lintel is lifted up" and becomes higher than at that time when "it was lifted up" and when it was said: "lift up the gates, your princes, and be lifted up, everlasting gates, and the king of glory shall enter in". "And the house was filled with smoke". From the remission of the fire the whole "house was filled". And "smoke" is the vapor of fire.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: When therefore I have done all these things, "the lintel was lifted up by the voice with which they cried out". It is a blessed thing, then, for each one of us so to labor that he may become a partaker of the door and of the "lintel" of the door, which is according to the understanding of Christ God. For it is not, I think, unseemly to say that the flesh is called the door and the Word the "lintel". "The lintel was lifted up by the voice with which they cried out, and the house was filled with smoke", with that good "smoke" from the "glory" of God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And I said: O wretched me, for I am pricked with compunction!". Before you "see the vision", do you not confess yourself to be "wretched", O Isaiah? He does not say: so long as "Uzziah" lived did it never come into my mind that I was "wretched"; for I begin to know that I am "wretched" when I "see the vision", when "Uzziah the leprous king" is "dying" for me, and I say: "O wretched me!"? Now I too begin to confess to the Lord and to say of my very self: "O wretched me!", as Isaiah says: "O wretched me!". And close to this the Apostle too says: "wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?". It is a blessed thing, then, that I should confess myself "wretched". If I humble myself and, repenting, weep over my sins, God will hear me and give me a deliverer, and I say: "thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!". In truth let us say from the heart: "wretched me". Let each one call to mind the causes of his miseries and his offenses, and let us say, rising to prayer, mindful indeed as though confessing, but forgetful as though no longer committing them, and let us say: "wretched me, for I am pricked with compunction!". He is not "pricked with compunction" before he "saw the vision", before "Uzziah died"; when he begins to do penance, at once he says: "for I am pricked with compunction". If anyone is without feeling "in respect of the inner man", though he be a sinner, he is not "pricked with compunction"; but just as, though you apply a goad to the outer members, the dead body does not feel it, in the same way also, even if you apply the divine words to a sinner who has been put to death through sin and does not do penance, he is neither sorrowful nor repentant, nor has he "the sorrow that works confession, the sorrow that is according to God". But if anyone wishes to be saved and hears the words of one reproving and correcting him, at once he says: "O wretched me". Nor does it suffice to say: "wretched me"; there must be added to it: "because I am pricked with compunction". And would that he might be "pricked with compunction" yet more! For the more we are "pricked with compunction", the more the bonds of our sins are loosed from us. On this account that Ahab gained no great profit, because he was not much "pricked with compunction", but he was indeed "pricked with compunction", yet only once. For which reason it was said: "have you seen how Ahab has been pricked with compunction!" But if anyone be such that he does not cease to be "pricked with compunction", he says likewise as the Apostle: "I am not worthy to be called an Apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God", and: "to me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given", and: "faithful is God, for Jesus Christ came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first". Do you see that he was much "pricked with compunction", not once but always—that in writing and speaking and acting he was "pricked with compunction"? As also Isaiah in the present passage, who says: "O wretched me, for I am pricked with compunction, because, since I am a man and have unclean lips, I dwell also in the midst of a people that has unclean lips". Note also another thing: that the sins of Isaiah were not also in deeds, but only in words; for which reason he says: "because, since I am a man and have unclean lips". But there was also "a people having unclean lips"; it did not befit him to accuse the "people" and to say that there were more sins in it than of "unclean lips".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And I said: O wretched me, for I am pierced with remorse, since, although I am a man and have unclean lips". I cannot suppose that Isaiah humbled himself; rather, the Scripture says and gives testimony that his "lips are cleansed" by "one of the Seraphim", who "was sent" to "take away his sins". And "one" of the "Seraphim" is my Lord Jesus Christ, who was sent by the Father to "take away" our "sins", and he says: "behold, I have taken away your iniquities and have cleansed away your sins". And do not think it an affront to his nature, if the Son is sent by the Father. Indeed, that you may recognize the unity of the deity in the Trinity, Christ alone in the present reading now forgives "sins", and yet it is certain that "sins" are forgiven by the Trinity. For he who has believed in one, believes in all. Let there be brought to me, then, from the heavenly altar the "tongs", that it may touch my lips. If the "tongs" of the Lord touch "my lips", it "cleanses" them. And if it "cleanses" them and "cuts away" their vices, as we said just now, I shall open my mouth to the Word of God, and no longer shall an "unclean" word go forth from my mouth, "since, although I am a man and have unclean lips, I also dwell in the midst of a people that has unclean lips". The "Seraphim" that was sent cleansed the "lips" of the prophet, but did not "cleanse the lips of the people". For he himself confessed that "he had unclean lips and dwelt in the midst of a people that has unclean lips". But this "Seraphim" that "was sent" did not judge any of the "people" worthy to have "their lips" too "cleansed", and therefore they still act impiously, therefore they still repudiate my Lord Jesus Christ, still curse him with "unclean lips". But I pray that the "Seraphim" may come and "cleanse" my "lips".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And I saw with my eyes the King, the Lord of Sabaoth". Why should we not set forth in the present a certain tradition of the Jews, plausible indeed yet not true, and why should we not find its solution? They say that Isaiah was for this reason sawn asunder by the people, as one transgressing the law and proclaiming things beyond the Scriptures. For the Scripture says: "no one shall see my face and live", but this man says: "I saw the Lord of Sabaoth". Moses, they say, did not "see", and you have "seen"? And for this reason they sawed him and condemned him as impious; for they did not know that "with two wings the Seraphim covered the face of God". "I saw the Lord". If Isaiah "saw the face", Moses also "saw". Moses "saw the back parts", as it is written; nevertheless he "saw the Lord", even though he did not "see" his "face". And so this man too "saw", although he did not "see" the "face". Wrongly, therefore, did they condemn the prophet. "And I saw with my eyes the King, the Lord of Sabaoth; and one of the Seraphim was sent to me". There is not one single coming of my Lord Jesus Christ by which he descended to the earth; he came both to Isaiah and to Moses, and to the "people" he came, and to each one of the prophets he came; and do not you fear: even though he has now been received up, he will come again. But that he came also before his coming in the flesh, receive as witness the one who declares and says: "Jerusalem! Jerusalem! you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you, how often have I wished to gather your children!". "How often have I wished". He does not say: I did not see you except at this coming, but he says: "how often have I wished". And turning himself through each of the prophets, saying, I was Christ, who spoke through the prophets: do not you fear; and now Jesus Christ is sent. He does not lie. "I am with you", he says, "all the days until the consummation of the age". He does not lie. "Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them". Since, therefore, Jesus Christ is at hand and stands beside us, and the high priest is ready and girded to offer to the Father our supplications, let us rise and through him offer sacrifices to the Father. For "he" is "the propitiation for our sins", "to whom is the glory and the dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!"

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And it came to pass in the year in which King Uzziah died, that I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up; and the house was full of his glory. And the Seraphim stood round about him, six wings to the one and six wings to the other; and with two they veiled his face, and with two they veiled his feet, and with two they flew. And they cried one to another and said: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Sabaoth, the whole earth is full of his glory", and the rest. But in order that we too may see the "vision" which Isaiah "saw", let us call upon Jesus, who has bestowed eyes upon those who do not see. For even now he can come and bring it about that we may behold with opened eyes the things that have been spoken in the reading of the sacrament; let us promise him that from now on we will no longer make "the body of Christ the body of a harlot", nor do works worthy of mourning. Let each one of us speak these things in his heart to God, and let us pray that his coming may take place even now; for if Jesus does not come, we cannot see these things. I pray that "a Seraph may be sent to me too", and that, "taking a coal with the tongs, he may cleanse my lips"; and why do I say "lips"? Isaiah was holy, and therefore only his "lips" were "cleansed", because he had offended only with his "lips", that is, in speech. But I am not such that I can say: "I have unclean lips"; I fear that I have an "unclean" heart, "unclean" eyes, "unclean" ears, an "unclean" mouth. As long as I sin in all these, I am wholly "unclean". If "I have looked upon a woman to lust after her, I have committed adultery with her in my heart". Behold, "unclean" eyes. If "out of my breast there go forth evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, false testimonies", behold, an "unclean" heart. "How beautiful are the feet of those who bring the gospel of peace, who bring the gospel of good things!". But I fear that, running toward evil, I have "unclean feet". "I stretch out" my "hands" to God, and perhaps "turning away his face" he says: "if you stretch out your hands, I will turn my face away from you". Who, then, cleanses me? Who "washes my feet"? Come, Jesus; I have filthy "feet"; for my sake become a servant, "pour your water into your basin", come, "wash my feet". I know that what I say is rash, but I fear the threat of him who says: "if I do not wash your feet, you will have no part with me". Therefore "wash my feet", that "I may have part with you". But why do I say: "wash my feet"? Peter can say this, who had need only that "his feet be washed"; for he was wholly clean. But I, since I have been washed once, need that baptism of which the Lord says: "I have another baptism to be baptized with". Why have we said these things? I am preparing both myself and my hearers for greater mysteries, if indeed the word of God comes, if it descends to us; for I fear that it may flee from me, that it may even disdain to bless me. The word once fled from the people because of "Achar", one sinner; the word fled, I say, from the people because of one sinner, "Achar the son of Zimri, the son of Zerah", from the "tribe of Judah", who was disobedient to God and therefore was "made anathema". And since now there is a multitude of people because of the preparation-day, and especially on the Lord's day, which is the commemoration of Christ's passion — for the resurrection of the Lord is not celebrated once a year, but always after every eighth day — pray to almighty God, that his word may come to us. Even if you are sinners, pray; God hears sinners. But if you fear that which is said in the Gospel: "we know that God does not hear sinners", do not be afraid, do not believe it: he who said this was "blind". Rather believe him who speaks and does not lie: "even if your sins be as scarlet, I will whiten them as wool; and if you are willing and hear me, you shall eat the good things of the earth". If you are "willing" even now to "hear", let us pray in common to the Lord, that at least now, at the coming of the Word, we may be able to give heed to the prophetic sayings.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
"And I saw with my eyes the King, the Lord of Sabaoth". If ever we have thought about God while we are still sinners, we too say what the prophet now says: "and one of the Seraphim was sent to me". How good is God! Because, He says, I hear Isaiah confessing—for he said: "O wretched me!"—because I hear him repenting—for he says: "I am pricked with compunction"—because he has declared his own offenses, saying: "since I am a man and have unclean lips, I dwell also in the midst of a people having unclean lips", I too, "while he is yet speaking, say: behold, I am present". "And one of the Seraphim was sent to me, and in his hand he had a coal". A "coal" is brought to the prophet, that through the burning of fire his "lips" might be purged, which had at some time sinned. Who is this "one of the Seraphim"? My Lord Jesus Christ: He, according to the dispensation of the flesh, was sent, having in His hand a "coal" and saying: "I came to send fire upon the earth, and would that it were already kindled!"

"And one of the Seraphim was sent to me, and in his hand he had a coal, which he had taken with tongs from the altar". Not by just any "fire" simply and by chance is the prophet purged, but by that which is "from the altar" of God. If you have not been purged by the "fire" of the "altar", there remains for you that fire of which it was said: "depart from me into the eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels". Not such is the "fire" that is "from the altar". All are to be delivered to the "fire", but not all to one "fire": some the "fire" "from the altar" awaits, others "that" which "is prepared for the devil and his angels".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: We read also in Isaiah that the prophet is purged by fire through "one of the seraphim, which was sent to him, when it took with tongs one coal from those which were upon the altar, and touched the lips of the prophet and said": "behold, I have taken away your iniquities". To me these things seem to be mystical and to indicate this, that to each one, according to that in which he sins, if he is worthy to be purified, coals are applied to his members. For since the prophet here says: "I have unclean lips, and I dwell also in the midst of a people having unclean lips", therefore the "coal taken up with the tongs" by the seraph purges his lips, in which alone he professes himself not to be clean. From which it is shown that only as far as the word was his sin found, but that in deed or work he had sinned in nothing; otherwise he would have said that I have an unclean body, or I have unclean eyes, if he had sinned in desiring the things of others, and he would have said: I have unclean hands, if he had polluted them with wicked works. But now, since perhaps in speech alone he was conscious to himself of that fault of which the Lord says: "that even for an idle word you shall render account in the day of judgment", because it is difficult even for the perfect to avoid the fault of speech, therefore the prophet too needed only the purging of the lips.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Let the reproving word, therefore, touch the "lips" of our mind and soul, that we too may say: "and it touched my mouth". If I shall have cleansed "my mouth", so that I speak nothing idle, nothing foolish, nothing base, nothing scurrilous—to name them all at once—nothing of those things that are forbidden, then I can say: "it touched my mouth". But so long as I "have unclean lips" and carry on unclean affairs, because of the words of sin "the fire from the altar does not touch me", nor "is one of the Seraphim sent to me".

"And He said: behold, this has touched your lips, and it has taken away your iniquities, and has purged your sins round about". Let the divine word bite us, let it burn up our souls, and let us say as we hear: "was not our heart burning within us?", that "our iniquities and sins may be taken away", and that, made clean, with clean mouth and clean heart and a whole clean conscience, we may give thanks to almighty God in Christ Jesus, "to whom is glory and dominion for ages of ages. Amen!"

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Isaiah, "seeing the Lord of Sabaoth seated upon a lofty and lifted-up throne", and "seeing" also "the Seraphim standing about him", and receiving the remission of sins through that fire which, brought "from the altar", "cleansed" his "lips" by its touch, says that "he heard the voice of the Lord" — not commanding, but rousing and "saying": "whom shall I send, and who will go to this people?" Then he says that "he answered" the Lord: "behold, it is I, send me". But when I take my place here and search into what is written, I find that Moses did one thing and Isaiah another. For Moses, chosen for the leading-out of the people from the land of Egypt, says: "provide another whom you may send", and he seems to contradict God; but Isaiah, not chosen, but "hearing": "whom shall I send, and who will go?", says: "behold, it is I, send me". It is worthwhile, therefore, for one "comparing spiritual things with spiritual" to inquire which of the two did better: Moses, who, after he was chosen, refused, or Isaiah, who, without even being chosen, offered himself to be "sent to the people". For I do not know whether anyone, attending to that contrariety of the affairs which appears in each, can say that Moses did the very same thing as Isaiah. So then I boldly make a comparison of these two holy and blessed men, and I decide and declare that Moses acted more modestly than Isaiah. For Moses was considering the magnitude of presiding over the people so as to lead them out of the land of Egypt, of contending against the "incantations" and sorceries of the Egyptians; on this account he says: "provide another whom you may send". But this man, not waiting to hear what would be enjoined upon him to say — even if he had been chosen — says: "behold, it is I, send me". Hence, because, being ignorant of what would be enjoined upon him, he says: "behold, it is I, send me", he is commanded to say those very things which were unwished-for by the one who was to say them. Or was it not undesirable, having been immediately bidden to prophesy, to begin from curses, saying: "with the ear you will hear and not understand, and seeing you will perceive and not see; for the heart of this people has been thickened" and the rest? Perhaps, then — if indeed it is expedient to say it boldly — he received as the wage of his rashness and boldness that he was commanded to say the very things which he was unwilling to prophesy. But since we have compared Isaiah and Moses, let us set up also another comparison closely akin, Isaiah and Jonah. The latter is sent "to preach" the overthrow of the Ninevites after "three days", and it irks him, unwilling to set out, to be the cause of evils for the city. But this man, not waiting for what would be commanded him to say, says: "behold, it is I, send me". It is good not to leap forward toward those dignities and offices of rule and ministries of the Church which are from God; would that we imitated Moses and said with him: "provide another whom you may send". For he who wishes to be saved comes to the rule of the Church not to lordship — even though he presides — but to servitude, if one must speak also from the Gospel: "the princes of the nations indeed lord it over them, and those who have power over them are called magistrates; but it shall not be so among you". For neither do "the princes lord it over you", but "whoever of you wishes to be greater shall be least of all"; "whoever wishes to be first shall be last of all". He, therefore, who is called to the episcopate is called not to lordship, but to the servitude of the whole Church. If you wish to believe from the scriptures that in the Church he who presides is the servant of all, let the Savior and Lord himself persuade you: such and so great a one became "in the midst of the disciples not as one reclining, but as one serving". For "taking a towel", after "he had laid aside his garments, he girded himself and, pouring water into a basin, began to wash the feet of the disciples and to wipe them with the towel with which he was girded". And teaching that rulers ought to be such as servants, he says: "you call me master and lord, and you say well; for so I am. If then I, the Lord and master, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet". The ruler of the Church, therefore, is called to servitude, so that from this servitude he may be able to go to the heavenly throne, as it is written: "you shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel". But hear also Paul, so illustrious a man, saying that he was the servant of all believers. "For I am the least of the Apostles, who am not worthy to be called an Apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God". Further, if this seems to prove not his servitude but only his humility, hear him saying: "we became little ones in your midst, as if a nurse should cherish her own children, though we could be burdensome as Apostles of Christ". It is expedient, therefore, that we be imitators of the humble words and deeds of the Lord himself and of his "Apostles", and do what was done by Moses, so that, even if someone is called to rule, he may say: "provide another whom you may send". "He says to God": "I have not been worthy since yesterday and the day before; I am of feeble voice and slow of tongue". And because "he said to God" humbly: "I am of feeble voice and slow of tongue", he hears from God: "who gave a mouth to man, and who made the deaf and dumb, the seeing and the blind? Is it not I, the Lord God?" Believe God and consecrate yourself to him. Although you are "of thin voice" and "slow tongue", hand yourself over to the word of God; you will say afterward: "I opened my mouth and drew in the Spirit". These things, indeed, on account of what Isaiah says: "behold, it is I, send me".

But let us in part take his side as well. For he willed, once he had received grace from God, not to receive it in vain, but to use it for what was needful. "Seeing the Seraphim", "seeing the Lord of Sabaoth seated upon a lofty and lifted-up throne, he said": "O wretched me, for I am pricked to the heart, because, being a man and having unclean lips, and dwelling also in the midst of a people having unclean lips, I have seen with my eyes the King, the Lord of Sabaoth". Saying this and making himself "wretched", he merits help, God taking up his humility. What is this help? "There was sent", he says, "to me one of the Seraphim, and he had in the tongs a coal which he had brought from the altar, and he touched my lips and said: behold, I have taken away your iniquities and have purged round about your sins". He obtained the benefit, being made clean and receiving the remission of sins. When he had heard: "whom shall I send to this people, and who will go for us?", it was not on account of his former conscience that he dared to say: "behold, it is I, send me", but because he had heard: "behold, I have taken away your iniquities". Therefore, since the saints are pricked to the heart and the inquiry is made between Moses and Isaiah, let us make satisfaction on behalf of Moses and also on behalf of Isaiah, giving to each of them from the scriptures his own portion. Moses did not receive the remission of sins, so as to say, as if already conscious of having been cleansed: "send me". On which account he says: "provide another whom you may send", for he had in his conscience the slaying of the Egyptian; and perhaps, being a man, he knew that he had also certain other sins, and therefore he refuses. But this man asks for the ministry not as one just by nature, but as one who has obtained grace. If Moses too had received a like grace and had heard: "behold, I have taken away your iniquities" and this: "I have cleansed round about your sins", perhaps he would never have said: "provide another whom you may send". There is, therefore, some reason both in Moses refusing and in Isaiah saying: "behold, it is I, send me".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: whom shall I send, and who will go to this people? And I said: behold, here I am; send me. And he said: go and say to this people: with hearing you shall hear and you shall not understand" and the rest. Concerning this discourse of the prophet Isaiah which has now been read, let us pray to God that he may grant us grace and that we may be able to expound things worthy of the prophetic spirit. "And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: whom shall I send?" After the prophet's "lips" had been cleansed, being prepared he took up the ministry of God and says: "behold, here I am, send me". But that he might be the more prepared for this, he remembered the voice of Moses. For Moses too, using the same words: "send me", was made "ruler of the people" and judge and was called "the servant of God".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
But let us look also at those things which the Lord commanded to be "said to the people": "go, and say to the people: with the ear you will hear and not understand, and seeing you will perceive and not see. For the heart of this people has been thickened, and with their ears they have heard heavily and have closed their eyes, lest at any time they see with their eyes and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart and turn back, and I heal them". Knowing that the hearing of words is twofold and recognizing a double constitution — that is, one of them bodily, the other spiritual — he says to "the people", prophesying about those things which were to be at the coming of Christ, that there would be a time when "they would hear and not understand" them, seeing that, when "they heard" my Lord Jesus Christ, they "heard" only the voice of the sayings, not the sense. And this is manifest from the fact that "he spoke in parables" "outside" to "the people", but "to the disciples in secret he unfolded" them. And he prophesies what came to pass: "with the ear you will hear and not understand". Further, that this was "prophesied" "to the people" about the coming of the Lord, the Savior himself says: "well did Isaiah prophesy about you, saying: "with the ear you will hear and not understand"". Let us grant, then, that "the people", listening to the words of the Lord, could not know what was said. But let us see what this is, which follows: "and seeing you will see and not know". Not everyone who "saw" those things which the Savior did was straightway, by "seeing", able to "understand" why they were done. Let us take, for example, "he washed the feet of the disciples", and they indeed "saw" well how the master "washed the feet" of "the disciples"; but others too who were present "saw" — yet only what was being done, not also why it was being done. For there was a likeness in the washing of "the feet" with which the Word of God "washed the feet of the disciples"; therefore the Savior says to Peter, who refused and said: "you shall not wash my feet", what does he say? "What I do you do not know now, but you shall know afterward". What, then, do "you do" now? says Peter; I see you "washing" our "feet", and the "basin" set, you "girded with a towel" and serving us and "wiping" our "feet". But because this was not the whole business — for indeed the Savior, stripped, "pours" spiritual "water into a basin" according to the scriptures and "washes the feet of the disciples", so that, when they have been made "clean", they may ascend to him who says: "I am the way", and not be full of the "dust" which he willed to be "shaken off" upon the unworthy and upon those who did not receive peace nor were worthy of the things which were spoken — and because this was what was signified, therefore he says: "what I do you do not know now, but you shall know afterward". And this was what was said in the rest: "you call me master and Lord, and you say well; for so I am. If then I, the Lord and master, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet". Does he then say this, that the bishop, "pouring water into a basin and having laid aside his garments and being girded with a towel", should "wash" my "feet" as I stretch them out, seeing that "you", he says, "ought to wash one another's feet"? If this is what is meant, none of us will keep the commandment; for no deacon or presbyter or bishop, "taking a towel", has "washed the feet" of any and all who come. But if you understand what is written, those who are truly blessed bishops, serving the Church, "pour water" from the scriptures into the "basin" of the soul, which is according to the scriptures, and attempt to "wash" and cleanse away and cast off the filth of "the feet of the disciples". And thus the bishops keep the commandment, imitating Jesus, and thus also the presbyters. Would that I too might now receive "water" which could "wash the feet" of your soul, so that each one of you, when he has been "washed", may say: "I have washed my feet, how shall I defile them?". For the bride says this in the Song of Songs, showing not bodily "feet washed", but "feet that do not stumble", of which Solomon says: "let your foot not stumble", and of which it is also written in the Psalms: "but my feet were almost moved". And moreover, those women who are appointed "widows" in the churches — "if", he says, "she has washed the feet of the saints". But if you wish to hear more plainly how the "widow washes the feet of the saints", hear Paul in another place appointing rules for "widows" and saying: "teaching well, that they may make the young women chaste", "washing the filth of "the feet" of the young women". And these "widows" are worthy of ecclesiastical honor, whoever they be that "wash the feet of the saints" with the word of spiritual teaching — "the saints", however, not males, but women; for I do not permit a woman to teach nor to rule over a man. He wishes women to be "teaching well, that" they may urge to chastity not young men, but "young women" — for it is unseemly that a woman become the teacher of a man — but that they urge "young women" to chastity and to "love their husbands and their children". Let us learn, therefore, to "wash the feet of the disciples". These things have been said on account of this: "seeing you will see and not know". For if anything was done by the Savior, by those indeed who "did not understand" it "was seen" with respect to the body, it was not "seen" with respect to knowledge; but by those who "understood" it "was seen" indeed with respect to the eyes, and it "was seen" also with respect to the understanding — so that this which was said, "seeing you will see and not know", was fulfilled not upon those who blessedly "see", but upon sinners. And we pray that, "seeing" all the things of the Gospels, we may "see" in a double manner how they were done with respect to the body, when our Savior descended to the earth; for indeed each thing that was done in the body was a likeness and a type of things to come. As, for instance, some man "blind from birth" recovered his sight; but truly this "man blind from birth" was the people of the Gentiles, to whom the Savior restored sight, "anointing" his "eyes" with his own "saliva", and sending him "to Siloam, which is interpreted sent". For he was sending those whom he "anointed" with the Spirit, that they might believe, "to Siloam", that is, to the Apostles and teachers, on which account it is written of "Siloam" that "it is interpreted sent". And as often as we begin to be visited by Jesus, so that we may receive the eyes of the soul, we are sent "to Siloam", that is, "sent". And so let each one of us, when he reads those things which were done in the Gospels, pray that this too be not fulfilled in himself: "seeing you will see and not know".

But if, as the simpler suppose, those things which were done were done not "on account of us", but merely done, and were not examples of another reality, let them explain how this which was said, "seeing you will see and not know", has any sense. For if those things which "were seen" did not have some sacred meaning, such that with the carnal eyes they were also spiritually beheld, he would never have said: "seeing you will see and not know". And for the proof of these things let us bring forward the testimony of another passage from the Gospel, which, according to those who follow the letter only, is a falsehood. Our Savior and Lord says to the disciples in the Gospel according to John: "if you believe, not only will you do the things which I do, but you will do even greater than these". Let us see, then, whether the disciples "did" any "greater" things. What is "greater" than to "raise the dead"? Who — I do not say of us, but of the Apostles — "raised the dead"? The history relates that Paul "raised Eutychus from the dead", and Peter "Tabitha, which is interpreted Dorcas". But these things, and others of this kind, you can find; yet where are the "greater" things? But the Savior also made "the blind" see again, and, what is "greater", those who had been born so: let them show whom they have beheld "blind" from the womb cured by the hands of the Apostles. And countless other things one can find from the Gospels, who seeks them, since neither did the Apostles "do greater things than these" nor did their successors. But the word of Scripture spoke some such thing as this: "than these things which I have done", the bodily ones, "you will do greater". "I made men rise from the dead" bodily, you "will make them rise from the dead" spiritually. I poured this perceptible light upon "the blind", you will give spiritual light to those who do not see. And down to this present day I see these signs, "greater" than the bodily ones which Jesus "did", being done through the most faithful disciples of Jesus. Do not "the blind" now "see" and "the lame walk" and "the lepers are cleansed" and the rest come to pass, if he who yesterday was "blinded", approaching an idol as though to God, today calls upon the living God, abandoning his former ways? Does not he who yesterday was "lame" on account of sin, now, through the teaching of the disciples, taught the true way, walk with steady foot; and he who yesterday "had a withered hand", idle for doing good, today, receiving back his "hand", has it living? If you see someone polluted and having leprosy in his soul suddenly repent, pricked to the heart by the word of teaching, let it not irk you to say that it is "greater" that this man be spiritually "a leper" cleansed than that some other be carnally purged. And these things indeed the discourse has poured forth abundantly, desiring to show what this is which was said: "and seeing you will see and not know".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Now I heard a certain Hebrew expounding this passage and saying that the prophet indeed willingly and readily took up the prophecy to the people, not knowing what he would have to say to them; but then, hearing the sad things that had to be announced to the people—that is: "with hearing you shall hear and you shall not understand" and the rest—in what follows he becomes more reluctant; and when the voice of God says to him: "cry out", he answers him and says: "what shall I cry?". But I think these things are prophesied concerning the Savior, because it was to come to pass that "hearing they should not hear and seeing they should not see". Moreover, what is said will become plainer if we consider a little the passage: "perceiving you shall look and you shall not see". It is of this kind. The Jews indeed at that time "saw" the blind receiving their sight, but the reason of the sight they did not know; they "heard" the "parables" which the Savior "unfolded to his disciples in secret", but they themselves "did not hear", not knowing the things that were said; on account of this, bearing witness against them, he said: "he who has ears to hear, let him hear!". For they were not deprived of these "ears", so that they "should not hear", but their inner "ears" were dulled for hearing. On account of this he preaches to them and through the prophet foretells the things to come, saying: "with hearing you shall hear and you shall not understand, and perceiving you shall look and you shall not see. For the heart of this people has been made fat".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
But what is the cause that the one hearing "does not understand and the one seeing does not see"? "The heart of this people", he says, "has been thickened". Since indeed this too must be understood, whence it comes, bodily and spiritual fatness are not the same, nor are bodily and spiritual thinness the same. For that which is bodily thick comes to be in the flesh, and a "fleshly heart" does me no harm if "it be thickened", nor does it profit if by illness or by whatever cause it be made thin. And I suppose that the fleshly "heart" of those who are held by fear becomes such. For as they waste away entirely from sickness, so they say that the thickness too, and whatever is fat about their "heart", is thinned out. What harm, then, does it do me if my bodily "heart" "be thickened"? And suppose too my "heart" be made thin — what profit do I have from that? But by a shared term with the bodily "heart", the ruling part of our soul is named, as is manifest from what is said in the Gospel: "blessed are the clean of heart"; for those are not "clean of heart" who have not within them blood or any bodily matter. But it was said: "blessed are the clean of heart" in the sense of "blessed" are those who have "a clean heart", the ruling part of the soul being named instead of "heart". Since, therefore, the ruling part of our soul, which is said to be in the bodily "heart", is either "clean" or unclean — and our "heart" is unclean indeed when "the worst thoughts go forth from" it, "murders, adulteries, thefts, false witness, blasphemies", but "clean" when there are holy thoughts and divine understandings and a pure mind — on this account it must be judged that it is said to be made thin by the "thin" and holy Spirit of him who is saved, but "thickened" by malice and choked in him who sins. For it is said of the "Holy Spirit", who is according to "wisdom", that he is "only-begotten, manifold, thin, mobile", and that the just man receives this "subtle spirit"; for this "spirit" differs from "all intellectual, clean, subtle spirits". The ruling part of the heart, therefore, is "thin" indeed insofar as it is spiritual, but fat insofar as it is concreted from the vice of bodily matter, full of bodily thoughts, which are under reproach. Thus it is said: "the heart of this people has been thickened". Understand: from this "the heart has been thickened", that there is nothing in it besides human and fleshly cares; for just as the matter of the body is fat, in the same way also are bodily understandings and thoughts. Wherefore, since two things are set before us — that the "heart is thickened" from worldly cares and made thin from spiritual solicitude, when one thinks of the things which are the Lord's, casting off the fatness from the "heart" and knowing that, if his "heart be thickened", he will neither receive the words of God nor see the sacrament of salvation — let us lay aside the thickness and take up that thinness which has been spoken of, so that we too may say, as the prophet: "my soul has thirsted for you; how manifoldly does my flesh thirst for you, in a land desert and pathless and waterless, so in the holy place have I appeared to you" — not as though I were "holy" by nature, but if the prudence "of the flesh" wastes away, and if the prudence "of the flesh" has been wasted, then "in the holy place I shall appear to you". These things in explanation of that which was said: "for the heart of this people has been thickened".

There follows: "and with their ears they have heard heavily". It does me no harm if I "hear heavily" bodily, nor does this become for me a cause that I should not hear the words of God. For just as bodily blindness does me no harm, if my soul has not been blinded, so neither does lightness nor heaviness of bodily hearing hinder me. But there is a certain heaviness of hearing which harms the soul of man. What is this heaviness which is in the hearing of the soul? Sin, according to the scriptures, is "heavy". On which account someone, perceiving his sins, says: "like a heavy burden they have been made heavy upon me". And because "iniquity" is heavy, on this account "it sits upon a talent of lead", as is written in Zechariah. But the Egyptians "were sunk like lead in the mighty water" not because they had "heavy" bodies, but because their souls "had been made heavy" by the "talent of lead upon which iniquity was sitting" — on this account "they were sunk like lead in the mighty water". The heaviness of "the ears", therefore, comes from sin, and the lightness from righteousness. What is it that makes the hearing "hear" not "heavily", but lightly? The "wings" of the Word, the "wings" of virtue; for indeed the "wings" of the Word bestow much lightness. "Who will give me wings like a dove's, and I shall find rest?" This the prophet says, praying not that he may receive the bodily "wings of a dove", but the "wings of the dove" of the Holy Spirit. And again Solomon says of the rich man: "but he equips for himself wings like an eagle, and he turns back into the house of him who presides over him". If, therefore, we take "wings", we shall hear lightly; but if we sin and are negligent about our wings and our "wings" fall away, we shall be "made heavy" and "shall hear heavily". "With their ears", therefore, the sinners "have heard heavily". All the Jews indeed who then "heard" the Savior "heard" him "heavily", and therefore did not believe. And down to this day, as many as, "hearing" the scriptures, have not "heard" the spiritual word, which is light, but the "letter", which is "heavy" and "kills", "hear heavily". And thus Scripture is heard in a twofold manner: by him who does not understand what is said, it is "heard heavily"; but by him who understands it, it is not only not "heard heavily", but rather keenly, whence one becomes an understanding hearer.

And yet another thing is prophesied about the people of the Jews and about all of us, if we sin. "And they have closed their eyes, lest at any time they see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart". Of those who do not "see", some are "blind" and on account of blindness do not "see"; some are "in darkness" and therefore do not "see"; but others are neither "in darkness" nor blind, but because they "close their eyes" they do not "see". And the divine Scripture knows these differences, which belong to the ruling part of our heart; for the Savior says "to those who are in bonds: come forth, and to those in darkness, that it may be revealed to them", and "to those sitting in the region and shadow of death: a light has arisen for them". These did not "see" for the reason that they were "in darkness", until "a light should arise for them". "Deaf ones, hear, and blind ones, look". These formerly did not "see" for the reason that they were "blind" by nature. But those who are outside these, and who, in comparison with "the blind" and those who are "in darkness", are much worse, are those who do not "see" for the reason that they have willingly "closed their eyes". And that this is so, as we have asserted, the Savior will be a witness to me, saying: "if you were blind, you would not have sin; but now you say that you see; your sin remains". And he says well: "you say that you see"; for truly "they say that they see" and have the possibility of "seeing", but, "closing their eyes", they do not "see". And if ever you see a soul ingenious for understanding, and swift and eager, that does not meditate on the words of God, know that it is not on account of blindness that it does not "see" those things which are contained in the scriptures, not because it is "in darkness", but because it "closes its eyes". If, therefore, you have heard Scripture saying to those who "close their eyes": "open your eyes and see rightly", "open your eyes from that which you had closed", then you will be able to "see rightly" and to consider the light of truth. And it accuses indeed those about whom the inquiry is made, why they "close their eyes, lest they see"; yet it does not also say this, that it is never expedient to "close" the "eyes" of the soul. For it is expedient, as Isaiah makes plain, saying in what follows: "who will announce to you the eternal place? He who walks in righteousness and speaks the true and right way, stopping his ears, that he may not hear the judgment of blood, closing his eyes, that he may not see iniquity". If it is going to happen that, opening the "eyes" of my soul, I "hear" and perceive base speech, it is better to "close" the entrances than to "hear" and understand things that harm. When, then, do I "close"? When evil things are spoken, so that I may not even understand them. When the words of God are to be seen, then "we turn back and" God "heals" us, sending the word which "heals" those who wish to be cured in Christ Jesus, "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!"

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Let us examine what this means, which is said: "for the heart of this people has been made fat". Everyone who is occupied in the cares of the present life has "a heart made fat"; for those who dwell among worldly things the "heart is made fat" no otherwise than as if they were being choked by thorns. For this reason the "heart" grows fat and cannot receive the notions of the more subtle spirit. Let us therefore flee from such cares, so that our heart, made thin, may become acceptable to God. Let us flee earthly business; for these are the things by which the "heart is made fat". On account of this the discourse of Moses was subtle (as is written of him in Exodus), because he said that whoever, on account of such subtlety, shall be "pure in heart, they shall see God". For by such eyes God is seen. There are three things that are said: "for the heart of this people has been made fat" and "with their ears they have heard heavily" and "they have closed their eyes". But the things said in this passage can also be understood otherwise, more plainly. For many people think, when they look upon the creatures and contemplate this world, that they see them. And why do I speak of people? Behold, the birds and the four-footed beasts see the sun and the moon and the whole heaven together with the choir of stars, but they do not understand their reasons; only the just and holy, comprehending them through the reason of the wisdom of God, look upon them. Therefore in the eighth Psalm David says: "for I shall see your heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have founded". For does the prophet not now "see the heaven and the moon"? But this, that he says: "I shall see", if we consider it, we shall be able to understand.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: As far as the wording goes, Ahaz acted modestly when he had been commanded to "ask a sign in the depth or in the height"; and he gave a reason why he was unwilling to "ask," for he said: "I will not ask, nor will I tempt the Lord." And yet for this modesty he is blamed, and it is said to him: "Hear now, O house of David: is it a small thing for you to offer a contest to men, and how do you offer a contest to the Lord?" Then this promise is spoken: "Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel." Let these things be expounded, and as for the rest we shall look at them as we have need, and in those matters too the grace of God, that they may be made manifest. He is bidden to "ask a sign," not simply, but "for himself"; for the word says: "ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God in the depth or in the height." The "sign" set before him is "the Lord," my Jesus Christ. For this is the "sign" which he is bidden to "ask for himself in the depth or in the height." "In the depth" indeed, because "he who descended is the very same"; but "in the height," because "he who ascended above all the heavens is the very same." Yet to me this "sign" that is set before me, my "Lord" Jesus Christ, "in the depth and in the height," is of no profit, unless the mystery concerning his "depth" and "height" comes to be for me. For when I have received the mystery concerning Christ Jesus, concerning his "depth" and "height," then I shall receive the "sign" according to the commandment of the Lord, and it will be said to me, as to one having in himself "the depth and the height": "Say not in your heart: who shall ascend into heaven? — that is, to bring Christ down. Or who shall descend into the abyss? — that is, to bring Christ back from the dead. The word is near you, mighty in your mouth and in your heart." Therefore it is enjoined upon us all that we "ask" this "sign" for ourselves, that the "sign" which "the Lord God gives in the depth and in the height" may become useful to us. But if there is anyone who knows how to use reasonable contemplation, let him recognize this, that what is said, "in the depth and in the height," is not said disjunctively; for it signifies this, that he is able to be both. "Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord in the depth and in the height." And in the promise too the Apostle said: "that we may know what is the depth and the height and the breadth and the length." "And Ahaz says: I will not ask." He was unbelieving; for it was said: "ask for yourself." But the people even to this day does not "ask a sign," and therefore does not have him, and the people "offers a contest to the Lord" — the people that does not receive my Lord Jesus Christ. Then another question follows. For when this man says: "I will not ask, nor will I tempt the Lord," and reckons it to be a temptation if he "should ask a sign," it is said: "Hear now, O house of David: is it a small thing for you to offer a contest to men, and how do you offer a contest to the Lord?" But he does not "offer a contest to the Lord," nor do I think that he "offers a contest" even "to men," the one who "asks a sign in the depth or in the height." For the "contest" is God's, namely how he may save man. Therefore he does not "offer a contest to the Lord" who "takes refuge in salvation"; but he who, while the Lord contends to save man, flees from salvation and withdraws far from the Lord, "offers a contest to the Lord." "Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel." The true text of the copies of this prophet says: "you shall call." Moreover in Matthew we know it is read: "and they shall call his name Emmanuel." We cannot say that we ought to make anything less of the prophet. But how does the Gospel have this reading? Whether it was by someone who did not understand and ran to the easier course, as has happened also in many other places, or whether perhaps someone might say that the Gospel was published so from the beginning? Let him who wishes deliberate. The prophet indeed manifestly has: "and you shall call his name Emmanuel." I have known a certain man who, reading at the opening of the scriptures of the Gospel, "and you shall call his name Emmanuel," said within himself: 'What is "you shall call"? Who "shall call"? "Ahaz"; and how can "Ahaz" hear concerning the Savior, who came after many generations: "you shall call his name Emmanuel"?' and so, in place of what is, "you shall call," he wrote: "they shall call." But see that it is not to "Ahaz" that it is said: "and you shall call his name Emmanuel," but to the "house of David"; see that it is manifestly said: "Hear now, O house of David: is it a small thing for you to offer a contest to men, and how do you offer a contest to the Lord? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel." If, therefore, at any time we do not understand what has been said, let us make nothing less of it nor run to the easier course, but let us wait for the grace of God to supply to us, through the illumination of knowledge, the explanation of the question — or else, again, let the grace of God, through whom it wills, illumine us, so that we may seek no further, but our question may be resolved; and if we are counted worthy of understanding from the Lord, he will the more readily plead our very cause. What, then, is the "house of David"? If "David" is Christ, as I have often proved, the "house of David" is we, the Church of God; and it is said to us who are the Church, that we should not "offer a contest to the Lord" as said above, but that, when the Lord gives a "sign," we should receive it. To us, not to the "house of David," are these things said. And it is prophesied that, if anyone is of the "house of David," he "shall call his name Emmanuel"; for at the coming of Christ our Church alone says of Christ: "God with us." These things having been explained, as the grace of the Lord has granted, let us now inquire into other riddles.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "Butter and honey shall he eat." How is it prophesied that Christ "shall eat butter and honey"? And even if this be expounded by the Lord's bestowing it, again the things that follow will press upon us other questions. And would that we all did that which is written: "Search the scriptures." Many things drawn from bodily foods are named in the scriptures for spiritual nourishment. "As newborn babes, desire the reasonable milk that is without guile." Therefore there is without doubt a "reasonable milk," and we ought to seek such "milk." Again, in Proverbs it is written concerning "honey": "finding honey, eat what is enough, lest perchance being full you vomit it up." And did the Holy Spirit take care about that "honey" which is commonly known, "lest perchance" we "eat" too much? But the Holy Spirit, surely knowing spiritual "honey," says: "finding honey, eat what is enough." But with what understanding did the Holy Spirit enjoin upon us that, "if we have found honey" — since "honey" is indeed findable — "we should eat what is enough"? "Go," he says, "to the bee and learn how she is a worker." And the prophets are found to be "bees," for they fashion wax and make "honey," and, if it is fitting for me to venture to say it, their "honeycombs" are the scriptures which they have left behind. And if you are willing, come to the scriptures and you will find "honey." But also: "eat honey," and again in Proverbs it is said: "for a honeycomb is good, that your throat may be sweetened." Do you suppose the Holy Spirit says this — "eat honey" — of that which is in common use, "for it is good"? I do not dare to say that the Holy Spirit enjoins upon me concerning bodily "honey": "eat honey." Behold, I do not have it, or else I am of such a nature that I cannot "eat honey"; by what reasoning does he say to me: "eat honey," and do not "eat" flesh, but "eat, my son, honey, for it is good"? If you see that the prophets are "bees" and their work "honey" or "honeycombs," then you will see how, in a manner worthy of the Holy Spirit, you may understand "eat, my son, honey, for it is good." If anyone meditates on the divine oracles and is nourished by the words of the scriptures, he fulfills the command that bids: "eat, my son, honey," and, doing what is commanded, he takes possession of the word that follows: "for it is good," because "good" is this "honey" which is found in the scriptures. And what is said, "go to the bee," is of this kind. There is, so to speak, a certain "bee" above the bees; and just as among bees there is a certain king who is named to be king, so the prince of the bees is my Lord Jesus Christ, to whom the Holy Spirit sends me, that "I may eat honey, for it is good, and his honeycombs, that my throat may be sweetened." And perhaps the finer letters will be "honeycombs"; but the "honey" is the understanding that is in them.
